title: Opening tunes and repeating pieces for dancers at Manny's
summary: Allen and Russell ask about the first tune played at Manny's, and about the old custom of playing a piece twice or more when dancers applauded. Lewis says it faded once dancing stopped.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: George Lewis, January 25, 1960, Reel 1. George Lewis, January 25, 1960.
George Lewis, January 25, 1960. Yeah, George's voice is the only one we really need to be good.

We'll ask him a question and he says yes and we won't be able to hear the question. Well, I was reminiscing last night about Manning's with you out there. Remember the first tune you always used to play is All I Do the Whole Day Through is Dream of You. What was that?
Well, I didn't notice, as you're in the time, Tawler was playing.
I think because he loved it better than anything else.
Really? It's all right. That was his favorite tune.

Yeah. I remember Bunk's band always used to start out at the same tune every night in New York, too. You always hurt the one you love. Always hurt the one you love. Is that because you all liked it or just something easy to get warmed up on? Something easy to get warmed up on.
That's about the whole thing about it.

One other thing before I forget, maybe interrupt the train of thought, but this idea of playing a piece twice quite often. Some dancers I used to go to here, they'd play almost every piece. They'd play it twice. As soon as they get through, if anybody applauds at all, they'd play it twice. Is that an old custom?

Well, that was an old custom because during the dance hall times, you know, when a ployer like that, well, you call it an end call. Yeah. But in the later years, it just won't win. You know, dances played out. There's no halls or anything to work in. And the old time, they just kept the...
Yeah. I like it. It's a nice idea. I mean, a piece is good, but I like to hear it two or three times. I just wondered, in the old days, they did that all the time then. That was done all the time.

Right on every tune, you know, that you played, if you got the applause, which you did during those days, you got a lot of applause. Excuse me. And then when Bunk went to New York, well, he had that habit, so he just kept it right going.
I know sometimes they play a piece two or sometimes three times. I think as many as four times. Did they do that in the old days, too? They played more than twice sometimes? Oh, yes.
Now, Kid Thomas still does that, but I noticed he never plays them more than about twice, huh?
Yeah. Sometimes three times. I remember in New York, sometimes they played them as many as four times. People would want to hear them, do they?

They'd want to hear them, and they were dancing, you see. Now there's no dancing going on, so it don't make much sense to play the same thing over. Probably you may play the same tune anyhow, three or four times a night. Yeah. Someone may come and ask to play a must-write rhyme with it, and the next set someone will come back and ask for the same thing. Before the set is over, someone will ask for the same thing.
